River instruments: stories from the navigation hall, English · river collection · 284 MB, Wi-Fi required, Hide chapters, A river pilots desk, Start at the pilots desk and examine the folded river chart beneath its glass cover. The opening voice explains how crews planned a passage around shifting sandbanks and why a familiar route still needed careful attention on every journey., Measuring the current, Beside the current meter, listen to a surveyor describe taking a reading from a small boat. The account connects the instrument to a practical decision about when to leave the landing, without asking you to perform a calculation yourself., The bridge watch, At the bridge model, follow the lookout route from one side of the deck to the other. A retired crew member recalls watching for a low marker while another person kept track of the approaching bend in the river., Soundings in shallow water, The sounding line display introduces a job that required patience and clear spoken signals. Listen while looking at the marked lengths on the rope, then compare the working line with the later mechanical instrument in the neighboring case., Keeping a voyage log, Pause at the open logbook and notice the short entries written beside each date. This chapter explains how observations about weather, repairs, and waiting at a landing could help the next crew prepare for the same stretch of river., Repairing a navigation lamp, The lamp bench shows the small parts a keeper carried when a light failed. The narrator follows one routine repair and describes checking the beam from the water, where an apparently bright lamp might still be difficult to recognize., Voices at the crossing, Listen near the ferry photograph to hear three short memories of the crossing. Each speaker describes a different task, and the pauses between their accounts leave time to compare the landing shown in the image with the route map., Reading the river today, End beside the modern river map and find the old crossing on its edge. The closing chapter describes which habits of observation remain useful, even when the crew also carries electronic charts and receives regular messages from the shore station., Wi-Fi only, Get audio

River instruments: stories from the navigation hall, English · river collection · 284 MB, Wi-Fi required, Hide chapters, A river pilots desk, Start at the pilots desk and examine the folded river chart beneath its glass cover. The opening voice explains how crews planned a passage around shifting sandbanks and why a familiar route still needed careful attention on every journey., Measuring the current, Beside the current meter, listen to a surveyor describe taking a reading from a small boat. The account connects the instrument to a practical decision about when to leave the landing, without asking you to perform a calculation yourself., The bridge watch, At the bridge model, follow the lookout route from one side of the deck to the other. A retired crew member recalls watching for a low marker while another person kept track of the approaching bend in the river., Soundings in shallow water, The sounding line display introduces a job that required patience and clear spoken signals. Listen while looking at the marked lengths on the rope, then compare the working line with the later mechanical instrument in the neighboring case., Keeping a voyage log, Pause at the open logbook and notice the short entries written beside each date. This chapter explains how observations about weather, repairs, and waiting at a landing could help the next crew prepare for the same stretch of river., Repairing a navigation lamp, The lamp bench shows the small parts a keeper carried when a light failed. The narrator follows one routine repair and describes checking the beam from the water, where an apparently bright lamp might still be difficult to recognize., Voices at the crossing, Listen near the ferry photograph to hear three short memories of the crossing. Each speaker describes a different task, and the pauses between their accounts leave time to compare the landing shown in the image with the route map., Reading the river today, End beside the modern river map and find the old crossing on its edge. The closing chapter describes which habits of observation remain useful, even when the crew also carries electronic charts and receives regular messages from the shore station., Wi-Fi only, Get audio

This chapter follows a small team preparing a heavy line, with pauses that let you examine the fibers and the worn wooden handles nearby., A shipwright workshop, Stand beside the half-built hull and look along the curve of its ribs. The shipwright describes choosing timber, checking a joint, and teaching an apprentice to notice a small gap before the outer planks were fitted., Work at the fish market, The market gallery brings together sellers, carriers, and the people who repaired baskets at the end of the day. Listen beside the weighing table, then look for the chalk price board before continuing into the next room., Signals across the water, At the signal cabinet, the narrator explains why a clear message mattered in poor weather. Short examples describe the flags and lamps without requiring you to identify every symbol, so you can listen while examining the original equipment., The engine room, Pause near the engine model and follow the route from the boiler to the propeller shaft. A mechanic recalls the rhythm of routine checks and explains how the crew recognized a change in the sound of a working engine., Letters from the voyage, The writing desk holds copies of letters sent home during long trips. This chapter reads brief passages about ordinary meals, changing weather, and missing family, with quiet intervals that give you time to inspect the handwriting on display., A changing waterfront, Finish at the large window overlooking the present harbor. The final voices discuss new jobs and familiar landmarks, inviting you to compare the view outside with the historical photographs on the adjacent wall before you leave the gallery., Wi-Fi only, Get audio
